source.title: Differentially Private Learning Beyond the Classical Dimensionality Regime
source.authors: Cynthia Dwork; Pranay Tankala; Linjun Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes error across dimensionality in robust linear regression and explicitly distinguishes a training-error double-descent-like pattern from test-error double descent; it also reports that the estimation-error spike is absent with fixed positive privacy perturbation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own theoretical predictions and synthetic simulations across dimensionality. The Figure 1 simulations use n × d = 1000 and average 100 simulations. The paper also cites double-descent results from other work; those cited results are not recorded as findings here. The private training-residual result is distinct from the test-risk versions and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper derives and simulates estimation error (equal to excess test risk under isotropic features) across the ratio d/n for Huber regression with and without privacy noise. Its own Figure 1 results show the non-private peak at d = n and its disappearance under objective perturbation. That is a new-setting result on the general double-descent curve (V4). The non-private formula is recovered from prior work (TAH18, HS23), but the authors re-derive it as the ν=0 case of their theorem and simulate it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' headline double-descent claim concerns training error: objective perturbation produces a previously unobserved double-descent-like spike there, distinct from the known test-error double descent. They also note the non-private estimation-error spike at d = n is an instance of double descent and does not occur for fixed ν > 0. Their main contributions are sharp error characterizations of DP algorithms in the proportional regime, plus a finding that output perturbation can outperform objective perturbation in some settings.
record.recipe_differences: The study gives theoretical asymptotic analyses and synthetic simulations for objective-perturbed Huber regression in the proportional dimensionality regime, rather than a deep-network model-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported error behavior changes with the privacy perturbation ν: the estimation-error spike is described for ν = 0 but not for fixed ν > 0, while the private training residual has a spike. The plots also vary regularization λ.

fits_no_version.finding: With objective perturbation, training residual error has a singularity of order 1/|δ−1| at d = n. Without perturbation the residual is 0 for n < d and rises monotonically to ε².
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Privacy perturbation can induce a double-descent-like spike in training (in-sample) error near the interpolation threshold.

record.problems: The principal results are asymptotic theoretical predictions, and the displayed plots use synthetic data rather than real-world data. The study's estimation-error measure is parameter error, not conventional test-prediction error; its clearest newly identified double-descent-like result is for training residuals.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant results were left out. The paper's cited double-descent findings from other work were excluded because they are not results of this study.

untested.parts: No deep networks and no model-size sweep at fixed n.
No epoch-wise curves. The DP-SGD section uses a fixed small number of steps and reports no fall-rise-fall over steps.
Not tested directly; the sample count is not varied at fixed d. The R1 formula implies error rises as n increases toward d from below, but the authors do not state or test this.
Only linear (Huber) regression shows the peak. The logistic results (Figure 5) are not discussed in terms of a peak. Whether the curve subsumes the classical U-shape is not tested.
λ is varied in Figure 1, but the text does not describe how λ affects the peak. Label noise, multiple peaks and optimal regularization are not analysed.

missing.what: Output perturbation (Figure 6, Corollary 6.1) shifts the whole non-private error curve up by ν². The non-private double-descent peak and second descent therefore persist under output perturbation, unlike objective perturbation.
How the d = n peak changes across λ = 10 to 10⁻⁵ in Figure 1, for both ν=0 and ν>0. These curves are only plotted and cannot be read from the text.

record.verdict_notes: Estimation error d⁻¹‖β̂−β⋆‖² with covariance I/d equals excess test risk; the authors call it out-of-sample test error. So linking R1/R2 to V4 is reasonable. The limiting formulas are heuristic (λ→0, L→∞), while the theorem covers fixed parameters. The axis changes n and d together, not model size at fixed n. The non-private result reproduces cited work (TAH18, HS23), which neither original source contains.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweep and test error.
Increasing sample count near a fixed model's interpolation threshold.

Only a robust linear-regression setting is studied; other model classes and whether the result subsumes the classical U-shaped curve are not tested. The reported metric is parameter estimation error, not a conventional test-prediction error curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across the size, epoch, and sample axes.

The study varies privacy perturbation and regularization in its analyses, but does not test label-noise or variance as the driver, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.

rows.subject: objective perturbation with Huber loss (robust linear regression)
rows.operation_detail: Analyze and simulate estimation error as the dimensionality ratio varies.
rows.measure: Squared parameter estimation error, (σ*)² = d⁻¹||β̂ − β⋆||²
rows.value: (σ*)² → δ/(1−δ) ε² if δ < 1; (σ*)² → ε²/(δ−1) + δκ²/(δ−1) if δ > 1
rows.uncertainty: not stated for the displayed λ → 0 and L → ∞ limit
rows.note: The authors describe the non-private estimation-error spike at d = n as an example of double descent. Figure 1 also compares theoretical predictions with means over 100 synthetic-data simulations; the plotted simulation setting has n × d = 1000.
rows.check: The δ>1 value is mis-transcribed. It should read ε²/(δ−1) + ((δ−1)/δ)κ², not ε²/(δ−1) + δκ²/(δ−1). With this value the error falls from +∞ just past δ=1 to a minimum, then rises toward κ². The x-axis varies n and d jointly (n×d = 1000 in Figure 1), not model size at fixed n. The λ→0 and L→∞ limits are heuristic simplifications; the theorem holds only for fixed λ, L > 0. The row is the study's re-derivation of a cited result plus its own simulations.

source_check.correct: For ν=0, after L→∞ and then λ→0: (σ*)²→δ ε²/(1−δ) for δ<1; (σ*)²→ε²/(δ−1)+((δ−1)/δ)κ² for δ>1.
source_check.locator_found: Section 1.1.1, p. 6, non-private limiting-error display; Figure 1 and caption, p. 7.
source_check.problem: The δ>1 signal term is transcribed incorrectly: its coefficient is (δ−1)/δ, not δ/(δ−1).

rows.subject: objective perturbation with Huber loss (robust linear regression)
rows.operation_detail: Analyze and simulate estimation error as the dimensionality ratio varies.
rows.measure: Squared parameter estimation error, (σ*)² = d⁻¹||β̂ − β⋆||²
rows.value: (σ*)² → δ/(1−δ) ε² + δ²/(1−δ)³ ν² if δ < 1; (σ*)² → +∞ if δ > 1
rows.uncertainty: not stated for the displayed λ → 0 and L → ∞ limit
rows.note: The authors state that the estimation-error spike seen for ν = 0 does not occur in the private case with fixed ν > 0. Figure 1 compares predictions and means over 100 synthetic-data simulations, with n × d = 1000.
rows.check: No second descent: the limiting error is +∞ for all δ>1 when λ→0. The 'spike' is absent because the overparameterized side diverges entirely, not because the curve is smooth. This holds only in the heuristic λ→0 limit; the finite-λ curves in Figure 1 cannot be read from the text.

relationships.condition: Non-private ridgeless Huber/linear regression (ν=0, λ→0), estimation error equal to excess test risk, isotropic synthetic features
relationships.reason: Error spikes at d = n and falls again just past it, matching the simulations in Figure 1 (R1). The text calls this the well-known double descent.
relationships.display_finding: Excess test risk spiked at d=n and declined just beyond it, with simulations matching the theoretical curve.

relationships.condition: Objective-perturbed Huber regression with fixed privacy noise ν>0, λ→0 limit
relationships.reason: The authors state the spike does not occur. Error is +∞ throughout δ>1, so there is no improvement past the interpolation point (R2).
relationships.display_finding: The interpolation spike was absent, and limiting error was +∞ throughout δ>1, with no post-interpolation recovery.

relation.reason: The study's own error equations and simulations compare non-private recovery with its failure under objective perturbation.

tranche.reason: R2 supplies a counterexample to unqualified V4: fixed positive objective-perturbation noise eliminates finite post-interpolation recovery in the stated limit, requiring the claim to be qualified.

source_check.notes: The displayed limiting formulas first take L→∞; the theorem itself assumes fixed positive L, λ and ν. Figure 1 uses finite L=10 and plots n/(n+d), which decreases as δ increases. The authors' novel double-descent-like finding concerns training residuals, distinct from the estimation-error results checked here.
